story: Adem Kalender is first author of an Atlas study (KAL2010) on how metformin acts. In cells lacking AMPK or the TSC1/TSC2 proteins, metformin and phenformin still inhibited mTORC1, and the effect needed the Rag GTPases. Two mouse models, one for cancer and one for diabetes, agreed that metformin can suppress mTORC1 without AMPK. PubMed lists Kalender at the University of Cincinnati.

story: Lingyan Jin is first author of an Atlas study (JIN2026B) in mice aged with D-galactose injections. Rapamycin in the diet lowered the animals' susceptibility to atrial fibrillation and eased changes in the structure and electrical behavior of the heart's upper chambers. The effect ran mainly through lower HIF-1 alpha activity and did not depend on mTOR, which is an unusual result for a rapamycin study. PubMed lists Jin at the Department of Cardiology, Second Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University.

highlights.JIN2026B: First author: reported that rapamycin reduced atrial fibrillation susceptibility in aged mice through HIF-1 alpha, independent of mTOR.

story: Su Bo was first author of a 2026 study that combined computer modelling with lab work on lung cancer cells. Gambogic acid, a natural compound, killed A549 lung cancer cells and triggered cell death. In the docking analysis it bound most tightly to AKT and to S6K1, a target downstream of mTOR. The study did not measure direct inhibition of the mTOR kinase and had no animal or human data. PubMed lists Bo at Xiangyang No.1 People's Hospital.

The paper showed that mTOR and the enzyme S6K1 move on and off a protein platform called eIF3 in a set order. When S6K1 is idle it sits on eIF3. After cell stimulation, mTOR with raptor arrives, phosphorylates S6K1, and S6K1 leaves to act on its targets. PubMed lists her at the Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School.

story: In human cells, mTORC1 on the lysosome adds a phosphate to TFEB at serine 211, which lets 14-3-3 proteins hold TFEB in the cytoplasm. When lysosome function is blocked, TFEB loses the phosphate and moves into the nucleus, where it switches on lysosome and autophagy genes. Roczniak-Ferguson is the first of eight authors, and PubMed lists the Department of Cell Biology at Yale. A 2013 Atlas paper carries the same given name but no affiliation, so it is not counted here.

story: This 2022 mouse study from the NIA Interventions Testing Program found that rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months gave male mice a longer lifespan than rapamycin alone in earlier cohorts. In females the combination did about the same as rapamycin alone. Captopril gave a small lifespan gain in females.

James Nelson is a middle author. PubMed lists him in the Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Barshop Institute, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio. Five other Atlas records under this name carry no affiliation and are not included.

highlights.STR2022: Middle author of the ITP combination study.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies at The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio, Texas, USA.

studies.title: Lifespan benefits for the combination of rapamycin plus acarbose and for captopril in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.finding: NIA Interventions Testing Program C2017 cohort. In MALE mice, rapamycin plus acarbose started at 9 months produced a longer lifespan than either of the two prior ITP cohorts treated with rapamycin alone, suggesting the combination is more potent than its components used separately. In FEMALES the combination was neither better nor worse than rapamycin alone, which the authors relate to the limited survival benefit acarbose alone had shown in earlier female cohorts. Captopril gave a small but significant lifespan increase in females (4-5%). story: Erik D Marchant was first author of a 2026 paper in Function (MARCHANT2026), from the Barshop Institute and Long School of Medicine in San Antonio. Mice lacking the GATOR1 component Depdc5 in muscle had constantly active mTORC1. Their muscle showed more inflammation, but glucose tolerance stayed normal, even on a Western diet. The result questions the idea that muscle mTORC1 overactivity alone causes insulin resistance.

highlights.MARCHANT2026: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology and the Barshop Institute at the University of Texas at San Antonio.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Cellular and Integrative Physiology, Long School of Medicine, University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas, United States.

studies.finding: Constitutive mTORC1 activation in mouse skeletal muscle (via GATOR1 complex KO) increases inflammatory markers but is not sufficient to impair glucose tolerance, indicating that additional metabolic inputs beyond muscle mTORC1 hyperactivation are required to drive glucose intolerance.

story: Morris E Feldman is first author of a 2009 paper in PLoS Biology. The team made two mTOR kinase-domain inhibitors, PP242 and PP30, and tested them in cells and animals. Unlike rapamycin they block mTORC2 as well, and PP242 shut down cap-dependent translation that rapamycin left running. PubMed lists him at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Department of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology, University of California San Francisco.

Together these two papers established a whole new drug class beyond rapamycin.

story: Zixin Sang was first author of a 2026 paper in the Atlas that asks how cells sense the amino acid methionine. PubMed lists the author at the Department of Chemistry of the Southern University of Science and Technology in Shenzhen and at Hong Kong Baptist University.

The team built a methionine analogue that can be locked onto the proteins that grab it inside living cells. With it they found that the enzyme PKM2 binds methionine in a separate pocket, not through its usual enzyme activity, and passes the signal to mTORC1 through the GATOR2 complex. This was cell work, not a study in animals or people.

highlights.SANG2026: First author: developed the methionine probe and identified PKM2 as a methionine sensor acting through GATOR2.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Chemistry, Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Catalysis, State Key Laboratory of Medical Proteomics, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, China

studies.title: "Trojan" Methionine Probe Reveals PKM2 as a Methionine-Sensing Protein in the mTORC1 Pathway
studies.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
studies.finding: Identifies PKM2 as a direct methionine sensor for mTORC1. A photoaffinity methionine analogue plus chemoproteomics showed that PKM2 binds free methionine through a distinct recognition pocket — independently of its glycolytic enzyme activity — and transduces methionine availability to mTORC1 via the GATOR2 complex. Complements SAMTOR (GU2017), which reads the methionine metabolite SAM rather than methionine itself, and suggests a route to a pharmacological "methionine pseudostarvation" state.

story: Christina Lee Chung was first author of a 2019 paper in GeroScience. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Dermatology at Drexel University College of Medicine in Philadelphia.

This was a small, exploratory, placebo-controlled trial in people over 40 with sun-aged skin. Thirty-six people enrolled and 17 finished. Rapamycin applied to the skin lowered the senescence marker p16 and raised collagen VII, and some participants showed visible improvement. Because the trial was small, it is early evidence only.

highlights.CHU2019: First author of the human trial in which topical rapamycin lowered p16 and raised collagen VII in skin.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Dermatology, Drexel University College of Medicine, Philadelphia, PA, USA.

studies.title: Topical rapamycin reduces markers of senescence and aging in human skin: an exploratory, prospective, randomized trial
studies.finding: A small human trial testing whether rapamycin can slow aging in a tissue you can actually see and biopsy - skin. Topical rapamycin significantly lowered the senescence marker p16 and raised collagen VII, with visible improvement in skin appearance. Early, small-scale evidence (17 of 36 completed) that topical rapamycin can reduce a senescence marker in human skin.

current.role: Co-author of two Berkeley studies on how lysosomal cholesterol feeds into mTORC1.

story: Douglas F Covey is a middle author on two Science papers from the Zoncu group at Berkeley, listed in PubMed at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis both times. Both papers are about cholesterol as a signal to mTORC1 in cultured cells.

The 2017 paper showed that cholesterol in the lysosome activates mTORC1 through SLC38A9. The 2022 paper identified LYCHOS, a lysosomal protein that senses cholesterol and passes the signal on by holding back the GATOR1 complex.

highlights.CAS2017: Middle author of the study showing lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via SLC38A9 and NPC1.
highlights.SHI2022: Middle author of the study identifying LYCHOS as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Developmental Biology and Biochemistry, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO 63110, USA.

studies.title: Lysosomal cholesterol activates mTORC1 via an SLC38A9-Niemann-Pick C1 signaling complex
studies.finding: Establishes lysosomal cholesterol as a nutrient input that drives mTORC1 recruitment and activation at the lysosomal surface. SLC38A9 is required for cholesterol-driven mTORC1 activation through conserved cholesterol-responsive motifs, and does so independently of its arginine-sensing function; NPC1, which exports cholesterol from the lysosome, binds SLC38A9 and restrains mTORC1 through its sterol transport function. Boundary: cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts, no organismal endpoint.

studies.title: Lysosomal GPCR-like protein LYCHOS signals cholesterol sufficiency to mTORC1
studies.finding: Identifies LYCHOS (previously annotated GPR155) as a lysosomal cholesterol sensor for mTORC1. Cholesterol binds the amino-terminal permease-like region; mutating that site impairs mTORC1 activation. At high cholesterol LYCHOS binds GATOR1 through a conserved cytoplasm-facing loop, and by sequestering GATOR1 it promotes cholesterol- and Rag-dependent recruitment of mTORC1 to the lysosome. Boundary: human cell lines and biochemistry, not an organismal phenotype.

story: Yi He is first author of an Atlas study (HE2026) on ANGPTL8, a hormone made in fat tissue. In a large group of people, higher blood ANGPTL8 went with older biological age and higher risk of death. In mice, deleting the Angptl8 gene lengthened life and lowered ageing markers in fat. In cells, ANGPTL8 bound AKT2 and switched on the AKT-mTOR-S6K pathway, which pushed fat cells into senescence. PubMed lists He at the Department of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, in Wuhan.

highlights.HE2026: First author: led the report that ANGPTL8 drives fat-cell senescence through AKT2 and mTOR, with human cohort data and Angptl8-knockout mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Endocrinology, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, Hubei, China.

studies.title: An ANGPTL8-AKT2-mTOR Axis Drives Adipose Senescence and Aging-Related Functional Decline
studies.finding: Identifies ANGPTL8 as an endocrine driver of adipose-tissue aging: circulating ANGPTL8 tracked with biological age and mortality risk in a large human cohort, and genetic deletion of Angptl8 in mice extended lifespan and reduced senescence markers. Mechanistically, ANGPTL8 binds AKT2 and drives the AKT-mTOR-S6K axis to promote adipocyte senescence; blocking that axis abolished the pro-senescent effect.

current.role: First author of a 2026 study of how the lncRNA LINP1 binds mTOR and limits radiation-induced senescence in skin cells.
current.sub: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University (PubMed affiliation, 2026)
story: Xiaoting Liang was first author of a 2026 study in Molecular and Cellular Biochemistry (LIANG2026). The long non-coding RNA LINP1 rises after radiation and binds the FAT domain of mTOR. That weakens the contact between mTOR and p53, so less p53 is phosphorylated and fewer skin cells turn senescent. The team tested keratinocytes and human skin samples kept in the lab.

highlights.LIANG2026: First author; PubMed lists the author at Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan City, 030001, China.

studies.title: LINP1 suppresses radiation-induced cellular senescence in keratinocytes by modulating the mTOR-p53 axis
studies.finding: LncRNA LINP1 binds the FAT domain of mTOR, reduces mTOR-p53 interaction and p53 Ser15 phosphorylation, thereby suppressing radiation-induced cellular senescence in keratinocytes and human skin.

current.role: First author of a 2026 study on a gut-tumour bacterium, kynurenic acid and resistance to PD-1 blockade in gastric cancer.
current.sub: Department of General Surgery, Nanfang Hospital · Southern Medical University, Guangzhou, China
story: Using patient tissue and mouse models, the study linked the bacterium Streptococcus anginosus to resistance to PD-1 immunotherapy in gastric cancer. Its product kynurenic acid raised ITGA2 and dampened an mTOR-dependent chain that supports CD8+ T cell killing. Blocking ITGA2 restored T-cell activity in the models. Ren is the first of ten authors, and PubMed lists the Department of General Surgery at Nanfang Hospital.

highlights.REN2026: First of ten authors on the study of kynurenic acid, the ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis and PD-1 resistance in gastric cancer.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of General Surgery & Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Precision Medicine for Gastrointestinal Tumor, Nanfang Hospital, Southern Medical University, Guangzhou, People's Republic of China.

studies.title: Streptococcus anginosus-associated kynurenic acid drives PD-1 blockade resistance through an ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis in gastric cancer.
studies.finding: Tumor microbiota-derived kynurenic acid drives resistance to PD-1 blockade in gastric cancer through the ITGA2-mTOR-CTSV axis: kynurenic acid induces ITGA2 and inhibits an mTOR-dependent cascade, which sustains cathepsin V expression and suppresses CD8+ T cell cytotoxic function.
